origin.fact: An Asian-bred discus cultivar created in the 1990s.
Developed by breeders in Malaysia and Hong Kong. Some transparent-coloured fry from Blue Turquoise stock grew into solid blue adults.

Selected from cobalt blue and turquoise lines to fix all-over blue and suppress pattern. The first stable fish came from Malaysian breeders in the mid-1990s, and Hong Kong farms later refined the body shape.
Hobby writers place it in the wave of new discus mutations from the late 1980s and 1990s, together with forms such as Marlboro Red.
It is not a wild form. Strains like Blue Diamond do not exist in nature.

looks.fact: Solid blue body with a bright red eye that contrasts with the blue. Breeders pay close attention to the red eye.
Good fish have no markings on the body, gill covers or fins, a solid blue body and red eyes. A slight yellow tint on the tail can occur.
Even metallic blue, from cobalt to turquoise, with no bars or pepper spots. This source says black eyes are typical and red-eyed fish are a newer separate form, which conflicts with other sources.
The blue is structural colour, so how it looks depends on the lighting. A matte black or deep blue background shows it best.
A little orange around the eyes and on the tail and dorsal fin tips is acceptable. Dull grey colour can be a sign of poor health.

lines.fact: A red-eyed solid blue type is described as a newer development, separate from black-eyed Blue Diamond.
An albino Blue Diamond form is traded.

keeping.fact: Basic needs are good water hygiene, a group of fish and a varied diet. Modern cultivars are less delicate than wild-caught discus and are not very shy.
Keep water soft, acidic, warm and above all stable, with minimal swings in pH, temperature or minerals.
Feed meaty, high-protein food such as worms plus good pellets and flakes. Juveniles eat 3–5 times a day and adults twice. Remove any food left after about 10 minutes.
About 300 L in a tall tank for six adults, with gentle filtered flow, weekly 50% water changes and daily 30% changes for juveniles.
Suggested tankmates are cardinal and rummy-nose tetras, sterbai corydoras and Amano shrimp. Avoid fast or fin-nipping fish, and keep angelfish out because of shared diseases.
Astaxanthin colour foods do nothing for the blue. Beef heart 2–3 times a week is fine.
Vietnamese shops recommend 28–30°C, pH around 7, keeping them in a group, and feeding bloodworms and beef heart.
Needs at least about 210 L (55 US gal), and 380 L or more is better. Not recommended for beginners.
One Vietnamese shop calls it gentle and easy to care for if water, temperature and diet stay stable.

breeding.fact: Pairs form from groups of six or more juveniles at about 14 months and spawn on slate or cones.
Breeds true: fry inherit the blue evenly. Crosses back to turquoise or cobalt give offspring with mixed patterns.
Some pairs are poor parents and may need help with artificial rearing.
Like other discus, fry first feed on the parents' skin mucus. Raising fry is the hardest part.

health.fact: Said to be more stress-sensitive than red strains and to fade to a dull greyish blue under stress. Possibly more prone to gill flukes after repeated shipping (the source hedges this).
A dark body that will not lighten can mean chronic stress or parasites. Quarantine new fish for four weeks.
Common discus problems include fin rot from poor water and internal parasites (white faeces).

buying.fact: Pick juveniles (7–9 cm) with even blue and no pale patches, a round body, clear eyes, upright fins and a strong appetite. White or grey belly patches tend to get worse as the fish grows.
Ask for the farm and batch of origin and whether the fish were quarantined after import.
Choose fish that are fully, brightly blue, not dull or grey, and check for parasites.
A Vietnamese shop price list: 5–6 cm for 160,000₫ up to 11–12 cm for 480,000₫.
Unusually vivid colour on very small discus can be a sign of colour-enhancing hormones. Treated fish fade later and may stay stunted.

controversy.fact: Reliable Aquatics, an Indian discus hatchery, criticises the trade's use of colour-enhancing hormones on discus. It says treated fish fade, grow stunted with less round bodies, and may become infertile when overdosed. The post is about discus in general, not Blue Diamond specifically.
Sources disagree on whether Blue Diamond should have red eyes or black eyes.
